content: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE), also referred to as the Yt blood group antigen, is an enzyme in humans that is encoded by a specific gene. This enzyme plays a critical role in the nervous system by hydrolyzing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions and cholinergic synapses in the brain. By breaking down acetylcholine, AChE effectively terminates signal transmission between nerve cells and muscles or within the brain. In addition to its role in the nervous system, acetylcholinesterase is also present on the membranes of red blood cells, where it serves as the Yt blood group antigen. The enzyme exists in multiple molecular forms, which share similar catalytic properties but differ in their oligomeric assembly and the way they attach to the cell surface. These structural variations are encoded by a single AChE gene, and the diversity in the enzyme's forms arises from alternative mRNA splicing and post-translational modifications, including the association of catalytic and structural subunits. The predominant form of acetylcholinesterase found in the brain, muscles, and other tissues is a hydrophilic species. This form assembles into disulfide-linked oligomers that interact with structural subunits containing collagen or lipids. Another form of the enzyme, which is alternatively spliced and primarily expressed in erythroid tissues, differs at its C-terminal end. This variant includes a cleavable hydrophobic peptide with a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor site, allowing it to associate with cell membranes via phosphoinositide (PI) moieties that are added post-translationally. Acetylcholinesterase is a critical target of nerve agents, which inhibit its function. By blocking the activity of AChE, these agents prevent the breakdown of acetylcholine, leading to continuous and unregulated muscle contraction throughout the body, a condition that can be life-threatening.
